item.title: Pacific Islands
item.description: Pacific nations are pushing for stronger regional cooperation and sustainable early warning systems as climate-related hazards continue to threaten communities across the region. The issues were highlighted at the Eighth Meeting of the Pacific Meteorological Council was officially opened at the Fa'onelua centre in Nuku'alofa today.
item.content:encoded:
Pacific nations are pushing for stronger regional cooperation and sustainable early warning systems as climate-related hazards continue to threaten communities across the region.

The issues were highlighted at the Eighth Meeting of the Pacific Meteorological Council was officially opened at the Fa'onelua centre in Nuku'alofa today.

Delivering the keynote address, Dr Viliami Latu said Pacific countries needed to ensure investments in meteorological and disaster infrastructure could be maintained long after development projects ended. He asked delegates to consider who would maintain weather and early warning systems five, 10 and 20 years after the projects that funded them had ended.

“An early warning system that cannot be maintained will eventually cease to be an early warning system,” he said.

Dr Latu said maintenance, replacement, insurance, lifecycle costs, national capacity and sustainable financing needed to be considered from the beginning of every investment.

“This is not simply a technical issue, it is a question of Pacific resilience, development and security.”

World Meteorological Organization Regional Office Director Ishaam Abader said strengthening meteorological services was ultimately about protecting Pacific communities.

“Strengthening weather, climate and water services is not only about science and technology,” Abader said.

“It is more importantly about protecting lives, supporting sustainable development, safeguarding livelihoods and enhancing resilience across Pacific communities.”

Dr Latu said future partnerships with development partners must ensure systems built with external support could eventually be operated, maintained and sustained by Pacific nations.

He said new satellite technology, forecasting systems and artificial intelligence would strengthen meteorological services, but technology alone would not make the Pacific “Weather Ready”.

“The most important investment we can make remains an investment in our people,” he said.

Dr Latu highlighted the role of meteorologists, hydrologists, technicians, observers, forecasters, disaster managers, communicators and communities in building resilience.

He also stressed regional cooperation, saying weather systems and natural hazards did not recognise national borders.

Pacific nations needed to continue sharing knowledge, observations, technology, expertise and resources while developing systems that reflected regional priorities, he said.

Dr Latu said the Pacific Meteorological Council provided an important platform for that collective work.

He challenged delegates to consider whether decisions made at the meeting would ultimately make Pacific communities safer.

“If the answer is yes, then our work is worthwhile,” he said.

Dr Latu said Pacific communities could combine traditional knowledge of the environment with modern science and technology to better understand and respond to hazards.

He said the goal should be a Pacific where communities understood the risks they faced, received warnings in time and could act before hazards became tragedies.

“That is the Pacific we should seek to build,” he said.

“A Pacific that is informed. A Pacific that is prepared. A Pacific whose systems are sustainable. And ultimately, a Pacific that is ‘Secure’.”

item.title: Only 30% of Year 6 students reach minimum reading standard
item.description: Children in Tonga came together this week, 8 September, to celebrate International Literacy Day through a special reading event highlighting the importance of literacy, language and inclusive learning. The event was hosted by Save the Children Australia and the Ministry of Education and Training ( MET ), in partnership with the Global Partnership for Education ( GPE ).
item.content:encoded:
Children in Tonga came together this week, 8 September, to celebrate International Literacy Day through a special reading event highlighting the importance of literacy, language and inclusive learning.

The event was hosted by Save the Children Australia and the Ministry of Education and Training ( MET ), in partnership with the Global Partnership for Education ( GPE ).

The programme included English poems presented by Meleane, a Year 4 student from GPS Mu’a; and Simione, a Year 6 student from GPS Fasi; on the themes of healthy living, wellbeing and drug awareness, alongside a Tongan language reading focused on literacy. The readings were accompanied by sign language interpretation, reinforcing the importance of ensuring learning opportunities are accessible to all children.

A Tongan reading was also presented through a speech on Literacy, by Year 6 student from Hilliard Memorial School, Fiapa’i.

During a discussion of recent Pacific Islands Literacy and Numeracy Assessment ( PILNA ) results, education stakeholders reflected on literacy outcomes in Tonga and the importance of continued action to strengthen foundational learning. The results highlighted both progress and ongoing challenges, reinforcing the need for sustained investment in literacy, quality learning materials and effective teaching practices to ensure all children can reach their full potential.

Director for Primary School Division, Mr Herbert Takeifanga, emphasised the importance of literacy in supporting children's learning and future success.

" Reading is the foundation of learning. When children develop strong literacy skills in their early years, they are better equipped to succeed throughout their education and beyond. Every child in Tonga deserves access to quality books and learning opportunities that inspire a lifelong love of reading. International Literacy Day reminds us that investing in literacy is an investment in our children's future and the future of our nation."

In Tonga, only 30% of Year 6 students reach the minimum reading standard, demonstrating the need for continued investment in literacy and foundational learning.

Through a partnership between the Education ( MET ), GPE , Save the Children and Library For All, Tonga is expanding access to reading materials that reflect local culture and experiences. The initiative is expected to deliver more than 300 book titles for Years 1-6, with approximately 40,000 books planned for distribution throughout Tonga.

Save the Children Tonga Country Lead, Lilieta Takau, said literacy remains fundamental to every child's education journey.

" The progress we are seeing in literacy has been made possible through strong partnerships and investment in education. However, there is still much work to do. As governments and development partners consider future education investments, it is critical that foundational literacy remains a priority. Every investment in reading is an investment in a child's future."

International Literacy Day is celebrated globally on 8 September each year. This year's theme, 'Literacy for People, the Planet and Prosperity', recognises the critical role literacy plays in creating opportunities for individuals, communities and nations.

item.title: Tonga hosts Pacific Meteorological meetings
item.description: Hosted by the Kingdom of Tonga, and guided by the theme, “Weather Ready for a Secured and Sustainable Pacific”, the eighth meeting of the Pacific Meteorological Council ( PMC -8) will be held from 10 – 14 September, followed by the fourth Pacific Ministerial Meeting on Meteorology ( PMMM -4) on 16 September. item.content:encoded:
Hosted by the Kingdom of Tonga, and guided by the theme, “Weather Ready for a Secured and Sustainable Pacific”, the eighth meeting of the Pacific Meteorological Council ( PMC -8) will be held from 10 – 14 September, followed by the fourth Pacific Ministerial Meeting on Meteorology ( PMMM -4) on 16 September.

Pre-meetings began today at the Tanoa Dateline Hotel, with the One Pacific Programme discussions between SPREP and Pacific NMHS Directors, followed by the meetings of the seven PMC Expert Panels.

The Pacific Meteorological Council is a specialised subsidiary body of the Secretariat of the Pacific Regional Environment Programme ( SPREP ), established to facilitate and coordinate the scientific and technical programmes and activities of Pacific National Meteorological and Hydrological Services ( NMHS s).

Mr. Salesa Nihmei, Director of SPREP ’s Climate Science and Information programme, which also serves as the Secretariat of the PMC , this year’s meetings mark a special milestone for the Pacific meteorological community, as they gather to reflect on the progress and achievements of the past ten years under the Pacific Islands Meteorological Strategy ( PIMS ) 2017 – 2026.

“We have come a long way since 2017 and have had many triumphs as well as challenges over the years. This week we gather together as a community to reflect on the path which has brought us to where we are today, and to chart the course for where we want to go in the next ten years,” Mr. Nihmei said.

The PMC -8 is hosted by the Kingdom of Tonga, and Mr. Laitia Fifita, Director of Tonga Meteorological Services, recognises that pulling off a meeting of this magnitude, with close to 300 participants from Pacific NMHS s, regional CROP agencies, development partners, tertiary institutions, and the private sector, is no small feat.

“We are grateful for the partnership between the Government of Tonga and SPREP which has enabled us to organise this series of meetings. The last time the PMC was in Tonga was in 2015, and we are proud to welcome the Pacific meteorological community back to our shores once again,” he said.

A series of pre-meetings began today at the Tanoa Dateline Hotel, with the One Pacific Programme discussions between SPREP and Pacific NMHS Directors, followed by the meetings of the seven PMC Expert Panels. These panels were established to provide technical advice to the Council on matters concerning the development of meteorological services in the region under each thematic area of the PIMS 2017 – 2026.

The panels met to finalise their recommendations that will go before the PMC proper on Thursday. This includes the Pacific Islands Communications and Infrastructure ( PICI ) panel, Pacific Islands Climate Services ( PICS ) panel, Pacific Islands Marine and Oceans ( PIMOS ) panel, Pacific Islands Education, Training and Research ( PIETR ) panel, Pacific Islands Aviation Weather Services ( PIAWS ) panel, Pacific Hydrological Services ( PHS ) panel, and Multi-Hazard Early Warning Services ( MHEWS ) panel.

A Pacific Media Mana Class will follow on Tuesday and Wednesday 8 and 9 September 2026 at the Tanoa Hotel, bringing together nine Pacific island journalists for a capacity-building workshop and training to help them better understand emerging issues and Pacific priorities on weather and climate. The two-day training is a partnership between SPREP and the Pacific Community ( SPC ) through the Climate and Oceans Support Program in the Pacific ( COSPP ac).

item.title: Police conference celebrates women in policing
item.description: Women police officers from Tongatapu and the outer islands gathered for their annual conference this week, to celebrate achievements, strengthen leadership, and shape the future of women in policing. Tonga Police Women's Advisory Network ( TPWAN ) officially opened its 2026 Annual Conference yesterday, 7 September, at Tonga Police Headquarters in Lo
item.content:encoded:
Women police officers from Tongatapu and the outer islands gathered for their annual conference this week, to celebrate achievements, strengthen leadership, and shape the future of women in policing. Women make up 40% of the Tonga Police workforce.

Tonga Police Women's Advisory Network ( TPWAN ) officially opened its 2026 Annual Conference yesterday, 7 September, at Tonga Police Headquarters in Longolongo, under the theme "Organisational Leadership and Future Proofing the Tonga Police Women's Advisory Network."

The theme reflects TPWAN 's commitment to developing strong leaders, strengthening professional networks, and ensuring women across Tonga Police are supported and empowered to reach their full potential.

The opening was attended by Tonga Police Commissioner Geoff Turner, Australian Federal Police ( AFP ) Deputy Commissioner Lesa Gale, members of the Tonga-Australia Policing Partnership, the Tonga New Zealand Policing Programme ( TNZPP ) team, and TPWAN members.

Commissioner Turner paid tribute to the contribution and legacy of women in policing, including the women pioneers whose courage, resilience and dedication had helped pave the way for future generations.

He said: "Today, we gather not only to acknowledge the role of women in policing, but to celebrate a legacy of courage, resilience and service that continues to shape the future of Tonga Police. Your presence matters. Your leadership matters. Your voice matters. You are not simply part of the police service-you are helping define its future."

Commissioner Turner acknowledged the leadership of Deputy Commissioner Sokopeti Faletau and TPWAN 's continued efforts to champion women within Tonga Police and contribute to the advancement of women in policing across the Pacific.

Tonga Police says women now make up almost 40% of their workforce, "representing a significant milestone in the organisation's commitment to equality, inclusion and opportunity.

The AFP has also contributed to the conference through co-funding the expenses of the three-day programme.

item.title: Oceania 7s Cup to feature Tonga in Rotorua
item.description: Tonga will compete at the Oceania Rugby 7s Cup 2026 alongside seven other men’s teams and five women’s sides in Rotorua with qualification places for the HSBC SVNS 3 series on the line. The men’s competition will include Fiji, New Zealand, Australia, Samoa, Tuvalu, Cook Islands and Niue. These teams will also compete for Oceania’s SVNS 3 qualification places.
item.content:encoded:
Tonga will compete at the Oceania Rugby 7s Cup 2026 alongside seven other men’s teams and five women’s sides in Rotorua with qualification places for the HSBC SVNS 3 series on the line.

The men’s competition will include Fiji, New Zealand, Australia, Samoa, Tuvalu, Cook Islands and Niue. These teams will also compete for Oceania’s SVNS 3 qualification places.

The Women’s Oceania 7s Cup, which doubles as the SVNS 3 qualifier, will include Cook Islands, Niue and Solomon Islands, Samoa.

Oceania Rugby president Richard Sapias said the tournament would provide an important platform for Pacific teams ahead of the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games and Brisbane 2032.

“This is a golden era for rugby in our region,” Sapias said.

He said support from the Australian Government through PacificAus Sports and legacy investment would also provide opportunities for high-performance, media and communications education and training for participating Pacific teams and staff.

New Zealand Rugby Sevens high-performance lead Hannah Porter said the tournament would give New Zealand players valuable international game time ahead of the 2026-27 HSBC SVNS Series.

Oceania Rugby general manager Frank Puletua said the tournament featured one of the strongest fields assembled, with SVNS qualification at stake for five member unions across the men’s and women’s competitions.

Bay of Plenty Rugby Union chief executive Mike Rogers said hosting the tournament would benefit rugby across the region, from grassroots clubs to high-performance programmes.

A six-team International Women’s Invitational will also be contested, with Fiji, New Zealand, Australia, France, Japan and the United States taking part.

The men’s competition will have quarter-finals and semi-finals, while both women’s competitions will progress to semi-finals before the finals session.

Oceania Rugby and New Zealand Rugby confirmed on Thursday that the tournament will be held at Rotorua International Stadium on 31 Ocotber and 1 November.

The Oceania 7s Cup will also operate alongside the second-tier Oceania 7s Challenge, with promotion and relegation providing a pathway for member unions to progress through the regional competition structure.

Saturday’s matches will begin at 9am with pool play across the three competitions, while Sunday will feature knockout matches and finals.

The tournament is the only international rugby sevens competition scheduled to be held in Aotearoa New Zealand this year.

The 2026 Oceania 7s Cup is being delivered by Oceania Rugby in partnership with New Zealand Rugby and RotoruaNZ.

item.content:encoded:
Global temperature rise is set to cross 1.5°C, likely within the next few years, pushing climate risks and impacts to increasingly dangerous heights, but it is still possible to bring temperatures down and achieve global goals in the Paris Agreement, according to a new United Nations Environment Programme ( UNEP ) report. Anticipated impacts include intensified extreme weather, ecosystem loss, and submersion of Small Island Developing States and low-lying coastal cities.

The report, ‘ Limiting Overshoot ’, identifies an ‘overshoot, peak, and decline’ pathway as the best remaining option to minimize the magnitude and duration of this overshoot and try to return to below 1.5°C as soon as possible.

“This summer’s scorching heat, raging wildfires and deadly floods are a warning of what lies ahead. We must make the overshoot above 1.5 degrees as small and short as possible. That demands an overshoot of ambition” said UN Secretary-General Antőnio Guterres.

This pathway would minimize peak temperature rise through immediate and sustained cuts to greenhouse gas emissions, including methane, on the road to net-zero, and bring down temperatures through long-term net-negative emissions, with carefully governed Carbon Dioxide Removal ( CDR ) – the process of removing carbon from the air and storing it through afforestation or other means – an essential part of the mix.

At the same time, following this pathway would involve adaptation actions that reduce vulnerability to the current, expected and unexpected impacts of climate change on societies, communities and economies – although there will likely be limits to adaptation and irreversible impacts, especially if peak temperatures are not minimized. The report stresses such a pathway would reduce risks and impacts, make adaptation less difficult and expensive, and increase the chances of lowering temperatures.

“There are no good outcomes if we remain above 1.5°C. Across the globe, extreme heatwaves are already proving that climate impacts will strike faster, hit harder, and last longer - costing more lives and causing deeper disruption,” said Inger Andersen, Executive Director of UNEP . “Now is the time we must double down on climate action. We can – and must – get on the right path. By cutting greenhouse gas emissions, strengthening resilience and adaptation, and ensuring exceedance of 1.5°C is as small and short as possible.”

The most optimistic scenario will see temperature rise peak at 1.8°C above pre-industrial levels, above the goal of limiting warming to 1.5°C set by the Paris Agreement. Most other scenarios predict higher peaks.

Above 1.5°C, risks and impacts will intensify with every extra fraction of a degree and every year. Severe damage to human health, food security, water supplies, nature, cities, infrastructure, and economies is expected.

The report warns that the likelihood of crossing irreversible tipping points increases with the magnitude and duration of higher temperatures. These include the destabilization of major ice sheets, degradation of the Amazon rainforest and disruption of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (the system of currents that moves warm surface water north and cold deep water south, playing a key role in regulating the climate). Some impacts may emerge abruptly, while others will accumulate over time.

Considering the scale of the risks and the co-benefits of climate interventions such as a rapid transition away from fossil fuels to renewable energy – improving air quality and public health, lowering energy costs and increasing access to electricity – the report urges accelerated, collective and global action to get on an overshoot, peak and decline pathway. How quickly and strongly this action happens will define the shape and trajectory of the pathway.

Strong political will and multilateralism, effective policies, inclusive governance, and finance are all important enabling conditions for action – and equity and justice must underpin all responses. Countries with greater responsibility for climate change should act the fastest with the greatest ambition.

The report also finds that mitigation and adaptation, which are mutually reinforcing, must advance together, while being responsive to emerging risks. Interventions that achieve both mitigation and adaptation goals – such as nature-based cooling – should be prioritized.

Adaptation set up now forms the foundation for efforts to come, but it must become transformational and responsive to evolving non-linear and abruptly arising risks – including those that will harm mitigation efforts.

The report emphasizes that net-zero is a milestone towards net-negative, with CDR needed in addition to, not instead of, sustained reductions in greenhouse gas emissions. However, CDR can only contribute credibly to a return below 1.5°C if peak warming remains well below 2°C and all residual emissions are reduced. Strong governance frameworks for CDR will be critical to allow responsible deployment and manage implications for environmental integrity, equity, scale.

Years of inaction mean that even if a return to below 1.5°C is secured, irreversible losses and permanently changed conditions are certain. Many communities may be forced to relocate or change livelihoods, while societies will face the challenge of re-adjustment. This raises issues of justice, power, and political legitimacy, which will require new, inclusive governance arrangements to resolve difficult issues.

This report is a reminder that an overshoot, peak and decline pathway is a next generation climate frontier, but one which cannot be left unattended to for the next generation to tackle. Immediate action is required for such a pathway to remain possible.
